slides.label: Curvature As Relative Acceleration
slides.notes: Open by changing the emotional meaning of curvature. It is not only a scalar attached to a point; it is the rule that makes initially nearby free-falling geodesics drift together or apart. The lecture route is from a family of geodesics to the Jacobi equation, then to constant-curvature signs, geodesic polar coordinates, velocity holonomy, and the small-circle defects recorded by the notebook.

slides.label: Neighbouring Geodesics Produce A Jacobi Field
slides.notes: Introduce the geometric object before the equation. A geodesic variation is a sheet of geodesics indexed by a parameter s. Looking along the central geodesic, the derivative in the s direction gives a vector field J that measures separation inside the tangent planes of the surface. The important point is that J is not a coordinate distance drawn in the page; it is a tangent vector field along the base geodesic.

slides.label: The Jacobi Equation Reads Like Force
slides.notes: Now give the equation its physical reading. The left side is covariant relative acceleration along the base geodesic. The right side is supplied by the curvature tensor acting on the separation vector and velocity. In flat space the force term vanishes, so neighboring geodesics keep a constant relative velocity. In curved space the sign and direction of R(J,T)T decide whether the family focuses or spreads.

slides.label: The Sign Of Curvature Controls Separation
slides.notes: The constant-curvature fan makes the sign convention inspectable. In the flat model a fan has Euclidean angle sum pi and linear separation. In positive curvature, geodesics bend back toward each other and triangle angle sums have excess. In negative curvature, geodesics pull away and angle sums have defect. The scalar equation j double-prime plus K j equals zero is the two-dimensional normal form of that behavior.

slides.label: The Saved Deviation Plot Is The Measurement
slides.notes: This saved figure translates the same story into a measurable defect from the flat formula. The gray line is K equals zero. The teal curve for K positive drops below the flat baseline because small geodesic circles and neighboring geodesics are tighter than Euclidean intuition predicts. The red curve rises above the baseline because negative curvature creates extra room and faster separation.

slides.label: Phase Space View Of The Jacobi ODE
slides.notes: The phase panel asks students to track both separation and the rate of change of separation. A Jacobi field is determined by initial position and initial relative velocity, just as a second-order ODE should be. The red sample points and teal ellipses are not decorative; they mark local data that the equation transports along the parameter.

slides.label: Polar Coordinates Make The Proof Local
slides.notes: Geodesic polar coordinates turn the visual fan into a single coefficient G. The angular coordinate vector is a Jacobi field, so the same equation appears as G rr plus K G equals zero with Euclidean initial behavior at the origin. This is the local proof engine behind the small circle expansions: curvature enters by changing the rate at which angular arcs grow.

slides.label: Velocity Holonomy Is The Same Force
slides.notes: Connect this chapter back to parallel transport. If velocities are compared around a tiny geodesic rectangle, the two orders of comparison differ by curvature. That failure to commute is another face of the Jacobi force term. The slide should make students see that relative acceleration and holonomy are not separate phenomena; they are two measurements of the same curvature operator.

slides.label: Small Circles Remember Curvature
slides.notes: Small geodesic circles are a quiet diagnostic for the same deviation. In Euclidean space circumference is two pi r and area is pi r squared. Positive curvature subtracts from both at the first nontrivial order, while negative curvature adds. The coefficients one sixth and one twelfth are the scalar shadows of geodesic deviation near the center.

slides.label: Lab Ledger And Takeaways
slides.notes: Close by turning the chapter into a reusable audit habit. The object is a geodesic family, the vector is the separation field, the equation is Jacobi deviation, and the checks are the saved plots plus JSON assertions. The main takeaway is that curvature can be felt dynamically as relative acceleration, seen visually in geodesic fans, and measured numerically through small-circle defects.
